pos: n. (a place marking the border of the Canaanites)
etymology: Hebrew Lesha, perhaps a fissure or a breaking through; named once, at Genesis 10:19.
biblical_def: Lasha marks the far corner of the territory of the Canaanites in the table of the nations. The families are listed first: “And the Arvadite, and the Zemarite, and the Hamathite: and afterward were the families of the Canaanites spread abroad” (Genesis 10:18), and then the ground they held is bounded: “And the border of the Canaanites was from Sidon, as thou comest to Gerar, unto Gaza; as thou goest, unto Sodom, and Gomorrah, and Admah, and Zeboim, even unto Lasha” (Genesis 10:19). The chapter closes the branch: “These are the sons of Ham, after their families, after their tongues, in their countries, and in their nations” (Genesis 10:20). Lasha stands at the end of a list that includes the four cities of the plain — Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboim — and Moses, writing after the fact, names them as a boundary while the reader knows what became of them. Three chapters later the same plain is described as a paradise by a man about to choose it: “And Lot lifted up his eyes, and beheld all the plain of Jordan, that it was well watered every where, before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, even as the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt, as thou comest unto Zoar” (Genesis 13:10).

Moses, writing the border of the Canaanites, names Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboim as landmarks — and adds, when Lot looks at them, the words before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah. Well-watered ground is not a verdict.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that prosperity and judgment can occupy the same acre, and that a choice made by what the eye sees may be a choice made against God.

pos: n. (a town of Judah; the home of Jehoiakim's mother)
etymology: Hebrew Rumah, height or exalted, from rum, to be high; named once, at 2 Kings 23:36.
biblical_def: Rumah is named once in Scripture, as the home town of the mother of one of Judah's worst kings: “Jehoiakim was twenty and five years old when he began to reign; and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Zebudah, the daughter of Pedaiah of Rumah” (2 Kings 23:36). The books of Kings and Chronicles are careful to record the mother of each king of Judah, and the verdict on the reign follows immediately: “And he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to all that his fathers had done” (2 Kings 23:37). The Chronicler gives the same two facts in one sentence: “Jehoiakim was twenty and five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem: and he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD his God” (2 Chronicles 36:5). And the end of it came quickly: “In his days Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up, and Jehoiakim became his servant three years: then he turned and rebelled against him” (2 Kings 24:1). Jehoiakim was Josiah's son. He burned Jeremiah's scroll a piece at a time in a brazier. His name means the LORD raises up, his mother came from a town called height, and he brought his kingdom down.

corruption_paragraphs: Josiah was the most thorough reformer in the history of Judah, and the son who followed him burned the word of God in a fire on the hearth. Scripture gives the mother's name and her father's town, as it does for every king of Judah, and then the verdict without softening. Grace does not run in the blood.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that each generation answers for itself, that the most faithful upbringing cannot regenerate a heart, and that rebellion against a heathen king is no proof of faith in the true one.

pos: n. (a city destroyed by the kings of Assyria, named in Sennacherib's boast)
etymology: Hebrew Retseph, a hot stone or a pavement, from ratsaph, to lay with stones; named at 2 Kings 19:12 and Isaiah 37:12.
biblical_def: Rezeph is one of the cities Sennacherib named to Hezekiah in the most famous act of blasphemy in the Old Testament. The argument was simple and, on its own terms, overwhelming: “Behold, thou hast heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all lands, by destroying them utterly: and shalt thou be delivered?” (2 Kings 19:11). Then the roll of the fallen: “Have the gods of the nations delivered them which my fathers have destroyed; as Gozan, and Haran, and Rezeph, and the children of Eden which were in Thelasar?” (2 Kings 19:12), and the mocking question about their kings: “Where is the king of Hamath, and the king of Arpad, and the king of the city of Sepharvaim, of Hena, and Ivah?” (2 Kings 19:13). Isaiah records the same speech: “Behold, thou hast heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all lands by destroying them utterly; and shalt thou be delivered?” (Isaiah 37:11). The reasoning was sound about the gods of the nations and wholly false about the God of Israel, and that was the error of it. Sennacherib had counted the LORD among the idols he had already beaten, and the angel of the LORD went out that night.

corruption_summary: All religions are reckoned alike; Sennacherib listed the LORD among the gods he had already defeated, and learned the difference in one night.
corruption_paragraphs: The Assyrian's argument is the argument of every age that counts religions as a single class: these gods did not save their cities, therefore no god will save yours. Gozan, Haran, Rezeph and Thelasar were real cities with real gods and they were really destroyed. The flaw was the premise that the God of Israel belonged on the list.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD is not one of the gods but the only God, that He answers blasphemy in His own time, and that a tally of fallen idols proves nothing about Him.

pos: n. (a city of the children of Eden, destroyed by Assyria; also written Thelasar)
etymology: Hebrew Tela'ssar, probably Assyrian, perhaps the hill of Asshur; written Telassar at Isaiah 37:12 and Thelasar at 2 Kings 19:12.
biblical_def: Telassar was a city of the people called the children of Eden, and it is named in Sennacherib's boast as one of the places his fathers had destroyed. Isaiah gives it in this form: “Have the gods of the nations delivered them which my fathers have destroyed, as Gozan, and Haran, and Rezeph, and the children of Eden which were in Telassar?” (Isaiah 37:12). Second Kings gives the same sentence with the other spelling: “Have the gods of the nations delivered them which my fathers have destroyed; as Gozan, and Haran, and Rezeph, and the children of Eden which were in Thelasar?” (2 Kings 19:12). The speech around it is unchanged in both accounts: “Behold, thou hast heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all lands by destroying them utterly; and shalt thou be delivered?” (Isaiah 37:11), followed by the sneer at the kings of the conquered: “Where is the king of Hamath, and the king of Arphad, and the king of the city of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivah?” (Isaiah 37:13). The Assyrian records make it probable that this was a place in Mesopotamia, in the region the Hebrews called Eden. Its name survives in Scripture only because a blasphemer used it as evidence.

corruption_paragraphs: The same speech is recorded twice in Scripture, and the city is spelled two ways. That is what happens when a foreign name is carried into Hebrew by two hands, and it is a mark of two independent records rather than one copied from the other. The sentence, the city list and the argument are identical.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the historical books and the prophets confirm one another, and that the names of cities a tyrant levelled are preserved in the book of the God he mocked.

pos: n. (a place in Babylonia from which exiles returned; also written Telharesha)
etymology: Hebrew Tel Charsha, probably mound of the craftsman or wood-hill; written Telharsa at Ezra 2:59 and Telharesha at Nehemiah 7:61.
biblical_def: Telharsa is one of the settlements in Babylonia from which a company of exiles came up, and the verse that names it reports a painful problem: “And these were they which went up from Telmelah, Telharsa, Cherub, Addan, and Immer: but they could not shew their father's house, and their seed, whether they were of Israel” (Ezra 2:59). They numbered six hundred fifty and two: “The children of Delaiah, the children of Tobiah, the children of Nekoda, six hundred fifty and two” (Ezra 2:60). Among them were men who claimed the priesthood: “And of the children of the priests: the children of Habaiah, the children of Koz, the children of Barzillai; which took a wife of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite, and was called after their name” (Ezra 2:61), and the outcome is stated without pity: “These sought their register among those that were reckoned by genealogy, but they were not found: therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood” (Ezra 2:62). Nehemiah's register, which spells the place Telharesha, tells the same story. Men who had come a thousand miles to serve at the altar were turned away from it because the paperwork was gone.

corruption_paragraphs: Six hundred and fifty-two people came up out of Babylon unable to prove they were Israelites, and among them priests who could not find their names in the genealogy. They were not accused of lying. They were put from the priesthood as polluted, because the office was not theirs to assume on the strength of wanting it. Ezra left the question to be settled later by a priest with Urim and Thummim.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God appoints to His ministry and men do not appoint themselves, and that the church must examine a claim to office rather than receive it on assertion.

pos: n. (a place in Babylonia from which exiles returned)
etymology: Hebrew Tel Melach, hill of salt, from tel, a mound, and melach, salt; named at Ezra 2:59 and Nehemiah 7:61.
biblical_def: Telmelah is a settlement in Babylonia whose name means hill of salt, and it heads the short list of places from which a doubtful company came up with the return: “And these were they which went up from Telmelah, Telharsa, Cherub, Addan, and Immer: but they could not shew their father's house, and their seed, whether they were of Israel” (Ezra 2:59). Nehemiah gives the same list with his own spellings: “And these were they which went up also from Telmelah, Telharesha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer: but they could not shew their father's house, nor their seed, whether they were of Israel” (Nehemiah 7:61). The number differs by ten between the two registers — Ezra counts six hundred fifty and two, Nehemiah “The children of Delaiah, the children of Tobiah, the children of Nekoda, six hundred forty and two” (Nehemiah 7:62) — which is what one expects of two counts taken at different times. Both agree on the outcome: “These sought their register among those that were reckoned by genealogy, but it was not found: therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood” (Nehemiah 7:64). A hill of salt is a barren place, and the men who came from it came with nothing to show.

corruption_summary: A ten-man difference between two registers is called an error; two counts of the same company taken years apart are expected to differ.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezra counts this company at six hundred fifty-two and Nehemiah at six hundred forty-two, and the discrepancy is a standing item in the lists of alleged contradictions. The two registers were made at different times, of a people in motion, some of whom died and some of whom were added. A document that matched to the man across a generation would be the more suspicious of the two.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's people returned from barren places at real cost, and that Scripture's records bear the ordinary marks of honest administration.

pos: n. (a place near Jerusalem, by the house of Millo, where Joash was slain)
etymology: Hebrew Silla, perhaps a highway or an embankment, from salal, to cast up a road; named once, at 2 Kings 12:20.
biblical_def: Silla is named once, and only to fix the spot where a king of Judah was murdered by his own servants. The historian closes the reign in the usual form: “And the rest of the acts of Joash, and all that he did, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?” (2 Kings 12:19), and then reports the end: “And his servants arose, and made a conspiracy, and slew Joash in the house of Millo, which goeth down to Silla” (2 Kings 12:20). The assassins are named: “For Jozachar the son of Shimeath, and Jehozabad the son of Shomer, his servants, smote him, and he died; and they buried him with his fathers in the city of David: and Amaziah his son reigned in his stead” (2 Kings 12:21). The Chronicler supplies the reason, which Kings leaves out: “And when they were departed from him, (for they left him in great diseases,) his own servants conspired against him for the blood of the sons of Jehoiada the priest, and slew him on his bed, and he died: and they buried him in the city of David, but they buried him not in the sepulchres of the kings” (2 Chronicles 24:25). Joash had been saved as an infant by the priest Jehoiada, reigned well while that man lived, and then had Jehoiada's son stoned in the temple court.

corruption_paragraphs: Joash was hidden in the temple as a baby, crowned at seven by the priest who saved him, and repaired the house of the LORD. When Jehoiada died he turned, and had Zechariah the son of Jehoiada stoned in the court of the house of God. His own servants killed him for that blood, and he was buried in the city but not in the sepulchres of the kings.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a man borrowing another man's godliness has none of his own, and that God requires the blood of His servants at the hands of those who shed it.

pos: n. (a place near Ai to which Israel was chased after the defeat)
etymology: Hebrew Shebarim, the breakings or the quarries, from shabar, to break; the AV margin offers the reading in Morad. Named once, at Joshua 7:5.
biblical_def: Shebarim is the point to which the men of Ai chased Israel in the one defeat of the conquest. The attack had been made in confidence and with a small force: “So there went up thither of the people about three thousand men: and they fled before the men of Ai” (Joshua 7:4). The rout is described with its cost: “And the men of Ai smote of them about thirty and six men: for they chased them from before the gate even unto Shebarim, and smote them in the going down: wherefore the hearts of the people melted, and became as water” (Joshua 7:5). Thirty-six dead is a small casualty list and a catastrophic one, because Israel had just walked through Jordan on dry ground. Joshua's response was not a council of war: “And Joshua rent his clothes, and fell to the earth upon his face before the ark of the LORD until the eventide, he and the elders of Israel, and put dust upon their heads” (Joshua 7:6). And the LORD's answer named the cause: “Therefore the children of Israel could not stand before their enemies, but turned their backs before their enemies, because they were accursed: neither will I be with you any more, except ye destroy the accursed from among you” (Joshua 7:12). One man had taken spoil from Jericho, and a nation broke at Shebarim.

corruption_paragraphs: Achan took a garment, silver and a wedge of gold, and hid them in his tent, and reasoned as every secret sinner reasons: that it touched no one. Thirty-six men died at Shebarim, and the LORD told Joshua He would not be with Israel any more until the accursed thing was destroyed from among them. Sin in a covenant people is never a private transaction.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the corporate reality of sin among God's people, the duty of discipline, and that a leader's first act after a defeat should be to fall on his face before the ark.

pos: n. (a stone by En-rogel where Adonijah held his coronation feast)
etymology: Hebrew Zocheleth, the serpent stone or the creeping stone, from zachal, to crawl; named once, at 1 Kings 1:9.
biblical_def: Zoheleth is the stone beside which Adonijah held the feast that was meant to make him king. His ambition is stated first: “Then Adonijah the son of Haggith exalted himself, saying, I will be king: and he prepared him chariots and horsemen, and fifty men to run before him” (1 Kings 1:5). Then the sacrifice and the guest list: “And Adonijah slew sheep and oxen and fat cattle by the stone of Zoheleth, which is by Enrogel, and called all his brethren the king's sons, and all the men of Judah the king's servants” (1 Kings 1:9). The verse that follows is the hinge of the chapter: “But Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah, and the mighty men, and Solomon his brother, he called not” (1 Kings 1:10). A man who must leave the prophet off the invitation list knows what he is doing. Nathan went to the one person who could reach David: “Wherefore Nathan spake unto Bathsheba the mother of Solomon, saying, Hast thou not heard that Adonijah the son of Haggith doth reign, and David our lord knoweth it not?” (1 Kings 1:11). The name of the stone is said to mean the serpent stone, which is a fitting address for a coronation held in the absence of the word of God.

corruption_summary: A movement is judged by its attendance; Adonijah had the king's sons and the men of Judah, and had left out the prophet on purpose.
corruption_paragraphs: Adonijah's feast had sacrifices, princes, officers and a crowd. It also had a deliberate omission: Nathan the prophet, Benaiah, the mighty men, and Solomon were not called. A gathering that must exclude the man who speaks for God in order to proceed has told you everything about itself.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that self-exaltation is not a calling, that God's choice of a successor is not settled by a feast, and that the absence of faithful witnesses from a religious assembly is the warning sign.

pos: n. (a place in the border of Benjamin, by Rachel's sepulchre)
etymology: Hebrew Tseltsach, of uncertain derivation, perhaps shadow or noontide; named once, at 1 Samuel 10:2.
biblical_def: Zelzah is the first of the three signs Samuel gave Saul to confirm his anointing. The anointing comes first: “Then Samuel took a vial of oil, and poured it upon his head, and kissed him, and said, Is it not because the LORD hath anointed thee to be captain over his inheritance?” (1 Samuel 10:1). Then the signs, in order and in detail: “When thou art departed from me to day, then thou shalt find two men by Rachel's sepulchre in the border of Benjamin at Zelzah; and they will say unto thee, The asses which thou wentest to seek are found: and, lo, thy father hath left the care of the asses, and sorroweth for you, saying, What shall I do for my son?” (1 Samuel 10:2); and the second: “Then shalt thou go on forward from thence, and thou shalt come to the plain of Tabor, and there shall meet thee three men going up to God to Bethel, one carrying three kids, and another carrying three loaves of bread, and another carrying a bottle of wine” (1 Samuel 10:3). And it all happened: “And it was so, that when he had turned his back to go from Samuel, God gave him another heart: and all those signs came to pass that day” (1 Samuel 10:9). Two men, a particular place, an exact message about lost asses — God's confirmations are usually that specific, and that domestic.

corruption_summary: Divine confirmation is sought in impressions; Samuel gave Saul a named place, a stated number of men and the words they would say.
corruption_paragraphs: Men look for guidance in feelings and open doors, and call a vague sense of peace a confirmation. What Samuel gave Saul was checkable: two men, at Zelzah, by Rachel's sepulchre, who would say that the asses were found and that his father was anxious for him. Three such signs, each with its particulars, and all of them came to pass that day.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God confirms His word by what can be tested, that He changes the heart of the man He calls, and that a whole kingdom turned on an errand after lost donkeys.
